column4: The parallel (“blue”) dollar trades far above the official rate. Exporters hold back their harvest, importers rush their purchases and prices adjust to the dearer dollar.
The central bank has almost no dollars of its own. It cannot defend the peso, cannot pay for energy and parts imports, and every debt payment becomes a crisis.
Argentine bonds yield thousands of basis points above US Treasuries. Nobody lends, companies cannot get credit and the debt becomes unpayable.
Everyone wants dollars at once. The price jumps day after day, shops mark up prices and the central bank burns reserves to stop the stampede.
Banks cap withdrawals of deposits. Savers bang pots on bank shutters and the economy grinds to a halt.
The country stops paying its foreign debt. International credit is cut off for years and a long renegotiation with bondholders and holdout funds begins.
Grassroots groups and the unemployed block roads, bridges and avenues every day to demand jobs, food and welfare.
The labour federation calls general strikes and mass marches. Transport stops, factories close and the government gets a clear message.
Gas runs short in winter and power in summer. The country imports LNG cargoes at a fortune and industry faces scheduled cuts.
The country is split into two halves that do not listen to each other. Every measure is a battle and half the electorate will never vote for you.
Good weather and good prices: soybeans, corn and wheat yield like never before and dollars pour in through the port of Rosario.
Vaca Muerta is producing at full tilt. Argentina goes from importing gas to exporting energy, and the energy balance brings in dollars for the first time in years.
Low inflation, a steady dollar and rising reserves. For the first time in a long while, Argentines can plan more than a month ahead.
